headline: Dry and warm through Friday, with highs in the upper 70s to mid 80s and gusty northeast winds peaking on Thanksgiving, while a big swell and exceptionally high tides bring coastal flooding Thursday morning; the one truly impactful storm of next week is a quick, potent one Tuesday night into Wednesday that could drop 1–3 inches of rain at the coast and 3–5 inches in the mountains.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Wednesday stays dry around Glendale and the LA basin as temperatures and dry winds blowing out from the interior (offshore winds) both increase. A Wind Advisory takes effect for parts of the mountains Thursday morning, and forecasters considered adding more areas tonight or Thursday morning beyond the central San Gabriel and Santa Susana Mountains but held off because of low confidence and minimal expected impacts.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: The offshore push peaks on Thanksgiving, with a Wind Advisory from 6 AM to 2 PM Thursday. Temperatures peak Friday in the upper 70s to mid 80s across the coast and valleys, including the Glendale area. Offshore winds weaken Friday and a light ocean breeze returns Saturday, dropping coast and valley temperatures 4 to 8 degrees, with little change farther inland.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Next week turns very active, but only the midweek storm looks truly impactful; a weaker system Sunday night into Monday morning should be relatively mild, as should another next Friday. The Tuesday night–Wednesday storm looks like a quick but potent cold front with about 6 to 8 hours of rain plus strong, gusty winds, potentially bringing 1 to 3 inches at the coast and 3 to 5 inches in the mountains. Most of the rain currently looks to fall overnight Tuesday into early Wednesday morning, with some showers likely lingering into Wednesday afternoon; snow stays mostly above 8,000 feet, with possibly a few inches down to 7,000 feet, and residents in sensitive areas should follow this one closely.

coast: A large, long-period west swell peaks through Thursday morning and combines with exceptionally high tides to bring large surf and moderate to significant coastal flooding, worst at the morning high tide and in low-lying spots with no protection from the ocean. The highest surf and worst flooding are expected on the Central Coast from Point Conception northward, the Ventura County coast and far eastern parts of the southern Santa Barbara County coast, where Coastal Flood and High Surf Warnings run until 3 AM or noon Thursday and High Surf Advisories then continue into Saturday; other beaches, including LA County, see somewhat lesser but still concerning impacts under Coastal Flood Advisories until noon Thursday and High Surf Advisories through Thursday. Expect strong rip currents nearly everywhere, strong along-shore currents, sneaker waves, heavy shore break, coastal erosion and a higher risk of damage to coastal structures, making swimming dangerous. Offshore, Small Craft Advisories run into Thursday (into early Friday for some waters): outer-water seas peak at 14 to 19 feet Wednesday and inner waters north of Point Sal at 13 to 17 feet, with strong winds in the western Santa Barbara Channel Wednesday, from Point Mugu to Santa Monica Thursday, and locally from the northeast Thursday into Friday; large breaking waves near harbor entrances can capsize small boats. Friday night through Sunday, winds stay mostly below advisory levels, though rough seas may linger offshore (40 to 70 percent chance) and the western Santa Barbara Channel has a 50 percent chance of strong winds Sunday afternoon and evening.
watch_for: Coastal flooding and dangerous surf at Thursday morning's high tide, worst on the Central Coast and Ventura County coast
Gusty northeast winds Thanksgiving morning; advisory areas could still be expanded
The Tuesday night–Wednesday storm: 1–3 inches at the coast, 3–5 in the mountains, and strong winds, especially for sensitive areas
confidence: Forecasters have low confidence on whether wind advisories need expanding Thursday, and while the midweek storm looks potent, its timing (currently mostly overnight Tuesday into Wednesday morning) and rain amounts are still days out and could change.
